context: The sorted integer array is nums = [1, 3, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 10, 12, 15], and target = 6. Five consecutive 6s occupy indices 2 through 6. The diagram shows the final positions of both pointers for each of the two boundary searches.
description: The left panel searches directly for the leftmost target. When the binary search for the insertion point ends, i is at index 2 (the first 6, highlighted in teal), and j is at index 1 (value 3). The left boundary for 6 is therefore i = 2.

The right panel uses a double-headed arrow labeled “Equivalent” to connect finding the rightmost target with finding the leftmost target + 1. A binary search for the insertion point of target + 1 = 7 ends with i at the first element greater than or equal to 7 (the value 10 at index 7). The pointer j = i − 1 lands at index 6, the last 6, highlighted in teal. The array contains no 7. Here, finding the leftmost target + 1 means calling the binary insertion-point function to find the leftmost position for a 7, i = 7.

frames.explanation: This equivalence relies on the elements being integers. Every element greater than 6 is at least 7, so the first position with a value of at least 7 is also the first with a value greater than 6. After computing j = i − 1, check that j is in bounds and nums[j] == target. If either check fails, target is absent and the code should return −1.
frames.title: Finding the right boundary using an insertion point

summary: In a sorted integer array, subtract 1 from the insertion index for target + 1 to get a candidate right boundary. Before returning it, check that the index is valid and the element there equals target.
title: Finding the right boundary using an insertion point
